'''''Mercurialis annua''''', '''annual mercury''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the spurge family [[Euphorbiaceae]]. It is native to the Middle East and the Mediterranean region, where it grows on bare, sandy soils.  Its seeds are dispersed by harvester ants, which remove an oily coating that delays germination. In recent centuries, annual mercury has spread to northern Europe and many other parts of the world as an agricultural and urban weed. It has been studied for its complex genetics and breeding system. The name is from the Roman god Mercury, due to its association with fertility.

== Description ==
Annual mercury is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[herbaceous plant|herb]] which typically grows to about 30–50 cm (exceptionally, up to 1 m) tall,<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015}}</ref> with an erect, branched stem that has two strong ridges along its length, changing sides at each node. The whole plant is more-or-less [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] and, when broken, it exudes a watery sap (not a white latex, as other Euphorbiaceae do). It is easily uprooted to reveal a bundle of thin, fibrous roots.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and have a short petiole about 1 cm long (exceptionally up to 4 cm), with tiny green stipules, 1–2 mm long, at the base. Each leaf is about 7 cm long by 3.5 cm wide, ovate with a pointed tip, and up to about 10 (range: 4–18) blunt teeth along each side, each with a [[hydathode]] at the tip.<ref name="Sell3" /><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>

Plants can be male, female or [[hermaphrodite]], giving rise to [[Dioecy|dioecious]], [[Monoecy|monoecious]], [[Gynodioecy|gynodioecious]] or [[Androdioecy|androdioecious]] populations, which is very unusual in the [[plant]] kingdom. Male plants have their flowers arranged at the tips of long stalks ([[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]]) arising from the leaf axils and projecting beyond the leaves. Female plants have their flowers in sessile clusters of 1–4 at the nodes of the branches, or on short (4 mm) pedicels. Hermaphrodite flowers, where these occur, have a similar arrangement to the female flowers. Sometimes these are functionally female, producing no pollen or even lacking [[stamen]]s entirely.<ref name=Pannell2004>{{cite journal|last=Pannell|first=J.R.|last2=Obbard|first2=D.J.|last3=Buggs|first3=R.J.A.|date=2004-08-01|title=Polyploidy and the sexual system: what can we learn from Mercurialis annua?|journal=Biological Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=82|issue=4|pages=547–560|doi=10.1111/j.1095-8312.2004.00340.x|issn=0024-4066|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Pannell2008>{{Cite journal |last=Pannell |first=J.R. |last2=Dorken |first2=M.E. |last3=Pujol |first3=B. |last4=Berjano |first4=R. |date=2008 |title=Gender variation and transitions between sexual systems in ''Mercurialis annua'' (Euphorbiaceae) |journal=Int. J. Plant Sci. |volume=169 |issue=1 |pages=129–139}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Perry |first=L.E. |last2=Pannell |first2=J.R. |last3=Dorken |first3=M.E. |date=2012 |title=Two's Company, Three's a Crowd: Experimental Evaluation of the Evolutionary Maintenance of Trioecy in ''Mercurialis annua'' (Euphorbiaceae) |journal=PLoS ONE |volume=7 |issue=4 |article-number=e35597 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0035597|doi-access=free |pmc=3330815 }}</ref>
[[File:Mercurialis annua kz06.jpg|thumb|Closeup of the male flowers after anthesis]]

Even in the north of its range, annual mercury can usually be found flowering all year round.<ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref> The flowers of both sexes have 3 [[Perianth|perianth segments]] which look like small yellowish-green petals about 2 mm long. The males have 8–12 stamens which are somewhat longer than the tepals, with yellow anthers that turn black after the pollen is released. Female flowers have two ovaries and two [[Stigma (botany)|styles]], with bristle-tipped [[tubercle]]s.<ref name="Sell3" />
[[File:Mercurialis annua kz6.JPG|thumb|Female plants typically do not have their flowers on long peduncles, but sessile on the branches and the tip of the stem.]]

The fruit is a capsule, or [[schizocarp]] up to about 4 mm long with a warty, spiky coat, which splits into two mericarps as it matures. Each mericarp contains one shiny brown seed which is about 2 mm in diameter and has a [[Elaiosome|caruncle]] at one end. These are explosively expelled from the mericarp as it dries and turns inside-out, being fired about 30 cm (small seeds might go as far as 130 cm) from the parent plant.<ref name=Lisci1997>{{Cite journal |last=Lisci |first=M. |last2=Pacini |first2=E. |date=1997 |title=Fruit and seed structural characteristics and seed dispersal in ''Mercurialis annua'' L. (Euphorbiaceae) |journal=Acta sociatatis botanicorum poloniae |volume=66 |pages=379–386}}</ref>
[[File:Mercurialis annua sl14.jpg|thumb|The fruits are covered with hair-tipped tubercles and consist of two mericarps, each with one seed.]]
[[File:Mercurialis annua-femelle bray-sur-somme 80 25062007 3.jpg|thumb|Female flowers on the main stem have a short pedicel (<1 cm) and 3 whitish tepals.]]

==Identification==
In Europe, the plant most resembling annual mercury is [[Mercurialis perennis|dog's mercury]]. They do not grow in the same habitat: annual mercury is a weed of waste ground, whereas dog's mercury is a woodland plant, but they can sometimes be found in proximity, for example along woodland paths. The main differences between them are that annual mercury is easily uprooted, has branched stems, and is almost hairless except on the leaf margins; whereas dog's mercury is rhizomatous, unbranched, and usually hairy all over.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name="Poland" />

{{Image frame|width=325|content=[[File:Mercurialis x2.jpg|320px]]|caption=Dog's mercury (left) vs. annual mercury (right)|align=center}}

''[[Acalypha australis]]'' may look similar but has large shield-like bracts under the female flowers ([http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012530 Flora of China]).

==Taxonomy and genetics==
''Mercurialis annua'' was named by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in [[Species Plantarum]] ([https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13830#page/477/ p. 1035]) in 1753. He classified it among the "enneandria" (the 9-stamened plants) and gave as synonyms ''Mercurialis caule brachiato, foliis glabris'' (the mercury with a branched stem and hairless leaves) in [[Hortus Cliffortianus]] and ''Mercurialis testiculata'' (the mercury with testicles) in Bauhin's [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/72114 Pinax Theatri Botanici]. Linnaeus also assigned it the astronomical symbol for the sun (☉), which was simply a code that meant "annual".
[[File:Mercurialis annua sl19.jpg|thumb|Fertile male flowers produce large quantities of yellow pollen.]]

The original name is still used today, but several synonyms have been coined over the years, including ''Mercurialis ambigua'' <small>L.f.</small> (1762), ''Discoplis serrata'' <small>Raf</small>. (1838), and ''Mercurialis monoica'' <small>(Moris) B.M. Durand</small> (1963). None of these is currently accepted.<ref name=GBIF>{{Cite web |date=4 November 2023 |title=''Mercurialis annua'' L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3062975 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref>

A large number of subspecies, forms and varieties have also been named over the years, but again they have not been widely adopted.<ref name="GBIF"/> Some of the variety within this species can be explained by the breeding system and the polyploidy.<ref name="Pannell2008"/> There are no known hybrids with other species.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref>

In most of Europe, ''M. annua'' is a diploid with a chromosome number 2''n'' = 16.<ref name="Sell3"/> In these areas, populations are always dioecious (although it is never hard to find individual plants which do not conform). In parts of southern Europe and north Africa, however, plants are sometimes tetraploid, hexaploid, or have even higher levels of ploidy, and it is also in these areas that monoecy, androdioecy and gynodioecy occur. Studies so far have failed to establish whether the sexual system determines the ploidy level, or vice versa, or even if they are necessarily linked.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pannell |first=J.R. |last2=Obbard |first2=D.J. |last3=Buggs |first3=R.J.A. |date=2004 |title=Polyploidy and the sexual system: what can we learn from ''Mercurialis annua''? |journal=Biological Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=82 |pages=547–560}}</ref>

Various authors have offered explanations for the name of the genus. [[William Allport Leighton|Leighton]] states that is named in honour of [[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]], because he first discovered its virtues.<ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W.A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref> If this is a reference to the magical herb [[Moly (herb)|moly]], which Mercury (as Hermes) gave to [[Odysseus]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Homer |title=The Odyssey |url=https://archive.org/details/the-odyssey-of-homer_202010/page/144/mode/2up?view=theater&q=moly |language=English}}</ref> it is unlikely to be the correct plant, because it doesn't have a black stem and white flower. Richard Mabey claims that the "true" mercuries are goosefoots, specifically ''[[Chenopodium bonus-henricus]]'', and that the name became attached to this genus because of a superficial resemblance between them.<ref name=mabey>{{Cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Flora Britannica |publisher=Sinclair-Stevenson |year=1996 |isbn=1 85619 377 2 |location=London}}</ref> However, [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]] was using this name in Roman times, drawing a comparison between the fruits of the plant and certain attributes of the deity.<ref name=Dioscorides>{{cite web | vauthors = Dioscorides P | author-link=Pedanius Dioscorides |title=De Materia Medica |url=https://ia802907.us.archiveclarke.org/16/items/de-materia-medica/scribd-download.com_dioscorides-de-materia-medica.pdf}}</ref>

The common English name simply separates it from perennial, or dog's mercury, ''[[Mercurialis perennis]]''. [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]] referred to it as French mercury.<ref name=Culpeper>{{cite book |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The Complete Herbal |date=1850 |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=London |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513}}</ref> Dioscorides<ref name="Dioscorides"/> and [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]] used the [[Ancient Greek]] name {{Lang|grc-Latn|linozostis}} and said it was called by the Romans ''herba Mercurialis mascula'' or ''M. testiculata''; and by the Egyptians ''aphlopho''.<ref>[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D25%3Achapter%3D18 Pliny the Elder, The Natural History, 25.18]</ref>

== Distribution and status ==
Annual mercury is native to the [[Middle East]] and countries bordering the [[Mediterranean Sea]], where it occurs in desert and semi-arid regions, and from which it has spread to disturbed, agricultural soils and urban areas around the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Mercurialis annua'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:352179-1 |access-date=8 November 2023 |website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref> In the [[Arabian Peninsula]] it is found on sandy soils in mountain valleys, at an altitude of 1,200 m, where it grows just 5 cm tall.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Collenette |first=Sheila |title=An Illustrated Guide to the Flowers of Saudi Arabia |publisher=Scorpion Publishing Ltd. |year=1985 |isbn=0 905906 45 4 |publication-place=London}}</ref>

It is present in all the mainland [[Departments of France|départements]] of France, where it is considered native, as well as [[Guadeloupe]] and [[Martinique]], where it is introduced. In all these areas it is considered to be common, and the [[IUCN Red List|conservation status]] is LC ([[Least Concern]]).<ref name=INPN>{{Cite web |title=''Mercurialis'' annua L. |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/108351 |access-date=8 November 2023 |website=Inventoire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref>

In Britain, annual mercury occurs mainly in the south and east<ref>{{cite book |last1=Perring |first1=F.H. | last2=Walters |first2=S.M. |title=Atlas of the British Flora |date=1962 |publisher=Thomas Nelson and Sons Ltd. |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> but it has spread north in the latter half of the 20th century, becoming roughly three times as widespread.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref> Towards the northern parts of its range it becomes an increasingly urban weed, possibly benefiting from the [[urban heat island]] effect, where it grows on pavements and rubble.<ref name="Lockton" /> The first British record was in 1538 by [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]] and, to judge from other early records, it was not common at that time.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W.A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref> Its [[IUCN Red List|conservation status]] is LC (Least Concern).<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Mercurialis annua'' L. |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vnd |access-date=5 November 2023 |website=Plant Atlas 2020}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Annual mercury is native to arid regions around the Mediterranean, where it can find bare, dry soil in which to grow. When the fruit is formed, it is dispersed by a three-stage process. Firstly the seeds are catapulted away by the exploding seedpods, typically travelling around 30 cm from the parent plant. When these seeds land, the vibration caused by the impact attracts harvester ants of the genus ''[[Messor]]'' (in Italy, the species ''M. structor'' <small>(Latreille, 1798)</small>) which immediately gather them up and transport them to their nests, up to 5 m away. There, the ants remove the [[elaiosome|caruncle]] and deposit the seeds in chambers within the nest. With the caruncle removed, the seeds are ready to germinate, but they will not do so until the third stage occurs, when the ant nest is destroyed by some external event such as animal disturbance, flood, or ploughing. The soil from the ant nest is particularly rich and friable, making a perfect seedbed for new plants. For this reason, annual mercury is especially common in agricultural land, where it behaves not as a ruderal colonist of bare ground, but as a specialised inhabitant of places with regular disturbance events.<ref name=Pacini1990>{{Cite journal |last=Pacini |first=E. |date=1990 |title=''Mercurialis annua'' L. (Euphorbiaceae) seed interactions with the ant ''Messor structor'' (Latr.), hymenoptera: Formicidae |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1438-8677.1990.tb01395.x |journal=Acta Bot. Neerl. |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=253–262}}</ref><ref name="Lisci1997" />
[[File:20160114Mercurialis annua3.jpg|thumb|Typical habitat in Northern Europe is in field margins and cultivated land.]]

In the north of its range, where harvester ants do not occur (and during the winter in the south), a different dispersal strategy occurs. The seeds of annual mercury have an extremely low germination rate while the caruncle is present, but continued exposure to water for 48 hours allows a proportion of the seeds to develop, over a long period of time (2 weeks or more, rather than just a day or two for the seeds from an ant nest). This allows the plant to act as a [[pioneer species]], moving into new areas of bare ground when carried by floodwater.<ref name=Pacini1990/><ref name="Lisci1997" />

The habitats it grows in include Eastern Mediterranean limestone screes ([[European Environment Agency|Eunis]] code H2.68), on old walls (J1.31), and on disturbed soils in [[Geranium purpureum|little robin]]/[[Cardamine hirsuta|hairy bittercress]], [[Chenopodiastrum murale|nettle-leaved goosefoot]], and [[Sisymbrium officinale|hedge mustard]] vegetation communities.<ref name="INPN" />

Annual mercury has spread across Britain from the south in recent centuries, initially as an inhabitant of warm micro-climates in urban areas.<ref>{{Cite book |last=White |first=J.W. |title=The Bristol Flora |publisher=R.A. Blackwell & Partners |year=1912 |location=Bath}}</ref><ref name="Crawley" /> Here it often grows at the base of walls where there also a rich supply of nutrients, along with such plants as [[Ballota nigra|black horehound]], [[Malva sylvestris|common mallow]] and [[Sisymbrium officinale|hedge mustard]].<ref name=Sinker>{{Cite book |last=Sinker |first=C.A. |title=Ecological Flora of the Shropshire Region |last2=Packham |first2=J.R. |last3=Trueman |first3=I.C |last4=Oswald |first4=P.H. |last5=Perring |first5=F.H. |last6=Prestwood |first6=W.V. |publisher=Shropshire Wildlife Trust |year=1985 |isbn=0 95086 371 8 |location=Shrewsbury}}</ref> Subsequently, it spreads to arable fields and waste ground, and it is described in the [[British National Vegetation Classification|National Vegetation Classification]] as occurring in OV6 [[Cerastium glomeratum|sticky mouse-ear]], OV9 [[Tripleurospermum inodorum|scentless mayweed]] and OV13 [[Stellaria media|chickweed]] communities.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 5: Maritime communities and vegetation of open habitats|year=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref> Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L=7, F=5, R=7, N=7 and S=0, which means that it grows in places that are well-lit, damp, neutral and richly fertile.<ref name="Plantatt">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT – Attributes of British and Irish Plants – Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref>

Although it is generally thought to be wind-pollinated, male annual mercury plants can produce tens of thousands of flowers in a growing season, and these give rise to vast quantities of pollen and nectar, so a single plant might be visited by hundreds of insects daily.<ref name=Yampolsky>{{Cite journal |last=Yampolsky |first=Cacil |date=1934 |title=The cytology of the abscission zone in ''Mercurialis annua'' |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2480881 |journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=279–289 |jstor=248088}}</ref>
[[File:Melampsora pulcherrima (07).jpeg|thumb|An annual mercury plant blighted by the fungus ''Melampsora pulcherrima'']]

If pests or diseases are specific to a particular plant, this can be strongly indicative of the place where that plant evolved. The fungus ''[[Aecidium]] marcii'' <small>Bubák, 1903</small> is found only on annual mercury and not in any European country except Turkey.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aecidium marcii – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/fungi/dikarya/basidiomycota/pucciniomycotina/pucciniomycetes/pucciniales/pucciniales-incertae-sedis/aecidium/aecidium-marcii/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref> This suggests a Middle Eastern origin rather than a pan-Mediterranean one. The gall-forming fungus ''Leveillula chrozophorae'' <small>Braun, 1984</small> is also restricted to the Middle East, but it is polyphagous on various species of the [[Euphorbiaceae|spurge family]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leveillula chrozophorae U.Braun |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3483895 |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref> However, ''Aleyrodes elevatus'' <small>Silvestri, 1934</small> is a whitefly which spends part of its lifecycle on mercury or [[Parietaria|pellitory]] and occurs throughout the Mediterranean.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aleyrodes elevatus – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/animalia/arthropoda/insecta/hemiptera/sternorrhyncha/aleyrodoidea/aleyrodidae/aleyrodinae/aleyrodes/aleyrodes-elevatus/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>

Throughout Europe, annual mercury is commonly infested with several non-specialist fungi such as the rusts ''[[Melampsora pulcherrima]]'' and ''[[Melampsora]] populnea'' agg., specifically the cryptic species ''M. rostrupii'' <small>G.H. Wagner</small>, which is known as the dog's-mercury rust in Britain. The former infests the stems with an orange coating,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Melampsora pulcherrima – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/fungi/dikarya/basidiomycota/pucciniomycotina/pucciniomycetes/pucciniales/melampsorineae/melampsoraceae/melampsora/melampsora-pulcherrima/ |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref> while the latter produces small black dots on the surface of the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Melampsora populnea'' |url=https://fungi.myspecies.info/all-fungi/melampsora-populnea |access-date=8 November 2023 |website=Fungi of Great Britain and Ireland}}</ref> Another rust-like infection is caused by ''[[Synchytrium]] mercurialis'' <small>(Libert) Fuckel, 1870</small>, which produces glassy, golden warts and can distort the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Synchytrium mercurialis'' (Libert) Fuckel, 1870 |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/fungi/chytridiomyceta/chytridiomycota/chytridiomycotina/synchytriomycetes/synchytridiales/synchytriaceae/synchytrium/synchytrium-mercurialis/ |access-date=8 November 2023 |website=Plant Parasites of Europe}}</ref><ref name=redfern>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207–531 |isbn=1 85153 214 5}}</ref> Other fungi that occur on this plant include ''[[Cercospora]] mercurialis'' <small>Passerini, 1877</small>, which causes mottling of the leaves, and the rusts ''[[Puccinia]] cynodontis'' <small>Lacroix, 1859</small> and ''P. isiacae'' <small>(von Thümen) Winter, 1887</small>.<ref name=miners>{{Cite web |title=Mercurialis annua – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superrosids/rosids/fabids/malpighiales/euphorbiaceae/acalyphoideae/acalypheae/mercurialis/mercurialis-annua/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>

Amongst the polyphagous insects that utilise annual mercury, amongst other plants, are the [[Ocnogyna baetica|winter webworm]] and the [[Hyles euphorbiae|spurge hawk-moth]], whose larvae eat the leaves, and the [[weevil]]s ''[[Tropiphorus elevatus]]'' and ''Kalcapion semivittatum'' <small>(Gyllenhal, 1833)</small>, whose larvae create a large, oval swelling inside the stem or the petiole. ''[[Laparocerus]] junonius'' <small>Machado, 2007</small>, ''L. rasus'' <small>Wollaston, 1864</small> and ''L. roudieri'' <small>Machado, 2007</small> have free-living larvae which feed on the roots of this and other species. Two aphids, the [[Aulacorthum solani|foxglove]] and [[Aphis nasturtii|buckthorn]], feed on the foliage, whilst the fly ''[[Liriomyza bryoniae]]'' is a leaf miner. The only beetle associated with it is ''Hermaeophaga cicatrix'' <small>(Illiger, 1807)</small>.<ref name="miners"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=''Mercurialis annua'' |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=3432 |access-date=8 November 2023 |website=Database of Insects and their Food Plants}}</ref>

==In culture==
[[File:Bronze herm MET DT6197.jpg|thumb|A bronze [[Herm (sculpture)|herm]]]]
A [[Herm (sculpture)|herm]] (in Rome they were known as "mercuriae") is a statue consisting of a square block of stone with the head of [[Hermes]] ([[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]]) and a prominent set of male genitalia. As the fruits of annual mercury resemble testicles, the association with mercuriae is apparent.

Ancient herbalists had many uses for annual mercury. [[Dioscorides]] observed the symbolism of the fruits, writing "the male has branches that are small and round, as though it were two little stones lying together." Following the [[doctrine of signatures]], he claimed that a paste made from the "male" plant would cause the conception of a male child, while "female" plants would have the opposite effect.<ref name="Dioscorides" /> Modern botanists would consider the plant that bears the fruit to be female but, as the odds of it working would have been about 50-50, this might not have mattered.
[[File:Mercurialis annua sl15.jpg|thumb|right|The characteristic shape of the fruits give rise to its name.]]

[[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]] was similarly confused about the biology of mercury plants, in the 17th century: "at every joint in the male Mercury two small, round green heads, standing together upon a short foot stalk, which growing ripe, are seeds, not having flowers." He considered it useful mainly for gynecological problems, and questioned its association with the god, writing "Mercury, they say, owns the herb, but I rather think it is Venus's, and I am partly confident of it too, for I never heard that Mercury ever minded women's business so much."<ref name="Culpeper" />

By the 20th century, the biology was understood, but confusion between annual and dog's mercury had brought the herb into disrepute. Dog's mercury is much more common than annual in Northern Europe, and [[Maud Grieve]] seems to have reassigned the medicinal properties to the former, saying that annual mercury "is now disregarded in England."<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref>

==Uses==
It is not known whether annual mercury is poisonous to humans or not. The closely related [[Mercurialis perennis|dog's mercury]] certainly is, as there are cases where people have mistaken it for an edible herb such as [[spinach]], and subsequently died. Similarly, livestock have been known to die after eating a type of mercury, but the species is not recorded.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref>

Although this is not a native plant in America, it is reported that some [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]] people of eastern Canada have used the juices of the plant as a balm for wounds.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Delâge|first=Denys|title=Aboriginality and Governance: A Multidisciplinary Approach|publisher=Theytus Books|year=2006|isbn=1-894778-24-3|editor-last=Christie|editor-first=Gordon|location=[[Penticton Indian Reserve]], [[British Columbia]]|pages=35|chapter=Aboriginal Influence on the Canadians and French at the time of New France}}</ref>
